title: The Transition Elements: Titanium to Copper

titles.topic: General Physical & Chemical Properties of the First Row of Transition Elements, Titanium to Copper
titles.subtopic: The Transition Elements: Titanium to Copper

blocks.md:
- **Transition elements **are d-block elements which form **one** or **more** **stable** **ions** with an **incomplete d subshell**
- They are all metals found in the d-block of the Periodic Table, between Groups 2 and 13

  - Sometimes they are referred to as transition metals
- Not all d-block elements are classed as transition elements: scandium and zinc, for example, are not classed as transition elements, despite being in the d-block
- **Scandium** is not classed as a transition element because:

  - It only forms **one **ion, Sc<sup>3+</sup>
  - The Sc<sup>3+</sup>ion has **no electrons** in its 3d subshell; it has the electronic configuration of [Ar]
- **Zinc** is also not classed as a transition element because:

  - It also forms only **one** ion, Zn<sup>2+</sup>
  - The Zn<sup>2+</sup> ion has a **complete** 3d subshell; it has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d<sup>10</sup>

blocks.text: The transition elements on the periodic table

blocks.alt: Periodic table with all three rows of the d-block highlighted in blue — scandium to zinc, yttrium to cadmium, and hafnium to mercury — against the unhighlighted s-block and p-block elements.
blocks.caption: The transition elements are in the central d-block on the Periodic Table

blocks.md:
- The transition elements all have **incomplete **d subshells
- There are five orbitals in a d subshell. Some of these orbitals may have similar **shapes **but different **orientations**, whereas others may have completely different **shapes**
- The five orbitals are

  - 3d<sub>yz</sub>
  - 3d<sub>xz</sub>
  - 3d<sub>xy</sub>
  - 3d<sub>x</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup><sub> - y</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup>
  - 3d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup>
- Note that students are required to sketch the shapes of the **3d**<sub>**xy**</sub>** **and **3d**<sub>**z**</sub><sup><sub>**2**</sub></sup>** **orbitals **only**

- The 3d<sub>yz</sub>, 3d<sub>xz,</sub> and 3d<sub>xy</sub> orbitals are orbitals which lie in the y-z, x-z and x-y plane respectively

  - They all have **four lobes** that point **between **the two axes

blocks.alt: Diagram showing the orientation of 3d orbitals: 3dxy lobes between x and y; 3dxz between x and z; 3dyz between y and z, on xyz axes.
blocks.caption: The 3dyz, 3dxz, and 3dxy orbitals all have four lobes which are similar in shape but point between different axes

blocks.md:
- The 3d<sub>x2 - y2</sub> orbital looks like the 3d<sub>yz</sub>, 3d<sub>xz,</sub> and 3d<sub>xy</sub> orbitals, as it also consists of **four lobes**
- The difference is that these lobes point **along **the x and y axes and **not **between them

blocks.alt: Diagram of a 3d(x²-y²) orbital with four green lobes along x and y axes. Labels show axes X, Y, Z, and text boxes note lobe orientation.
blocks.caption: The four lobes in a 3dx2-y2 orbital point along the axes

blocks.md:
- The 3d<sub>z</sub><sup><sub>2</sub></sup> orbital is different from the other orbitals, as there are two main lobes which form a **dumbbell shape**
- The two main lobes point **along** the z-axis and there is a “doughnut” ring around the centre

blocks.alt: Diagram of a 3d_z^2 orbital with lobes along the z-axis and a toroidal shape around the origin. Axes labelled X, Y, Z for orientation.
blocks.caption: The 3dz2 orbital has a dumbbell shape with a ring around the centre

blocks.md:
- Although the** transition elements** are metals, they have some properties unlike those of other metals on the periodic table, such as:

  - Variable **oxidation states**
  - Behave as **catalysts**
  - Form **complex ions**
  - Form **coloured compounds**

- Like other metals on the periodic table, the transition elements will lose electrons to form positively charged ions
- However, unlike other metals, transition elements can form more than one positive ion

  - They are said to have **variable oxidation states**
- Due to this, Roman numerals are used to indicate the oxidation state of the metal ion

  - For example, the metal sodium (Na) will only form Na<sup>+</sup> ions (no Roman numerals are needed, as the ion formed by Na will always have an oxidation state of +1)
  - The transition metal iron (Fe) can form Fe<sup>2+</sup> (Fe(II)) **and **Fe<sup>3+</sup> (Fe(III)) ions
- The table below shows the most common oxidation states of a few transition metals

blocks.text: Oxidation states of transition elements table

blocks.md:
- Another characteristic property of transition elements is that their compounds are often **coloured**

  - For example, the colour of the [Cr(OH)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3-</sup> complex (where the oxidation number of Cr is +3) is **dark green**
  - Whereas the colour of the [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> complex (where the oxidation number of Cr is still +3) is **purple**

blocks.text: Colours of common transition metal complexes

blocks.alt: Ten test tubes with coloured solutions, each labelled with their chemical formula. Colours include purple, green, pink, and blue.
blocks.caption: Examples of some transition metal ions and their coloured complexes

blocks.md:
- Since transition elements can have variable oxidation states, they make excellent **catalysts**
- During catalysis, the transition element can change to various oxidation states by gaining electrons or donating electrons from reagents within the reaction

  - For example, iron (Fe) is commonly used as a catalyst in the Haber Process, switching between the +2 and +3 oxidation states
- Substances can also be adsorbed onto their surface and activated in the process

- Another property of transition elements caused by their ability to form variable oxidation states is their ability to form **complex ions**
- A complex ion is a molecule or ion, consisting of a central metal atom or ion, with a number of molecules or ions surrounding it
- The molecules or ions surrounding the central metal atom or ion are called **ligands**
- Due to the different oxidation states of the central metal ions, a different number and wide variety of ligands can form bonds with the transition element

  - For example, the chromium(III) ion can form [Cr(NH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup>, [Cr(OH)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3-</sup> and [Cr(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>]<sup>3+</sup> complex ions
